summary: Adds explanation, examples and guidance to the revised Expedited Forwarding definition in RFC 3246, written during clarification of the older RFC 2598. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Expedited Forwarding is the queueing behaviour that gives a flow a low-loss, low-latency, low-jitter service. Its original definition was too vague to implement against, so it was rewritten in RFC 3246. This memo explains the rewritten definition in more detail, shows how a router's scheduler affects the numbers in it, and works out the delay bound for several common scheduling algorithms.

questions: why was rfc 2598 ef definition replaced
what is the ef latency term
subtitle: Extra explanation, worked examples and scheduler guidance for the revised Expedited Forwarding definition.

tldr.problem: The original definition of the Expedited Forwarding behaviour was too vague to build against, and the revised definition in RFC 3246 is short on explanation.
tldr.mechanism: The memo restates the revised definition as two pairs of equations, one about the aggregate of EF traffic and one about individual packets, explains what the two error terms mean and why both are needed, and works out the delay bound for several common schedulers.
tldr.outcome: It adds no new functions to the EF behaviour, so it adds no security issues of its own. The memo is Informational and supplements RFC 3246.

facts.label: Error term for the EF aggregate

today: RFC 3247 is an Informational memo that supplements the revised Expedited Forwarding definition in RFC 3246, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It says it adds no new functions to that behaviour and therefore no security issues. The original, less precise definition it replaces is in RFC 2598.

sections.title: Why a Supplemental Document
sections.content:
The Expedited Forwarding per-hop behaviour was designed to be used to build a low-loss, low-latency, low-jitter, assured bandwidth service. Because of the great value of this behaviour, the memo argues, it is critical that the forwarding behaviour required of and delivered by a compliant node be specific, quantifiable and unambiguous.

Unfortunately, the definition in the original RFC 2598 was not sufficiently precise. A more precise definition is given in RFC 3246, and this memo is intended to aid understanding of the properties of the new definition and to provide supplemental information not included in the text of RFC 3246, for the sake of brevity.

The memo restates the definition, discusses some of its properties, covers the issues associated with per-packet delay and loss, and then discusses the impact of known scheduling architectures on the critical parameters of the new definition and the impact of real devices deviating from the ideal output-buffered model.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version of the EF definition was not precise enough for two vendors to build the same router from it. RFC 3246 replaced it with a tighter definition, and this memo is the commentary that was left out of that document for brevity.

sections.title: The Formal Definition
sections.content:
A node that supports EF on an interface at some configured rate R must satisfy two equations. The first, the aggregate one, says that the actual departure time of the j-th EF packet, d_j, is at most its target departure time f_j plus an error term E_a, for every j above zero. The target departure times are defined iteratively: f_0 and d_0 are zero, and f_j is the maximum of the arrival time a_j and the minimum of the previous departure d_j-1 and the previous target f_j-1, plus the packet length l_j divided by R.

In this definition d_j is the time the last bit of the j-th EF packet to depart actually leaves the node from the interface, f_j is the target departure time, that is the ideal time at or before which the last bit should leave, a_j is the time the last bit of that packet actually arrives at the node, l_j is the packet size in bits measured on the IP datagram without lower layer overhead, R is the EF configured rate at the output in bits per second, and E_a is the error term for the treatment of the EF aggregate, giving an upper bound on the difference between actual and ideal departure times for every packet.

The values d_0 and f_0 do not refer to a real packet departure and are used purely for the recursion, and the time origin should be chosen so that no EF packets are in the system at time zero. For the definitions of a_j and d_j the last bit of the packet includes the layer 2 trailer if present, because a packet cannot generally be considered available for forwarding until such a trailer has been received.

An EF-compliant node must be able to be characterized by the range of possible R values it can support on each of its interfaces while conforming to these equations, and the value of E_a that can be met on each interface. R may be line rate or less, and E_a may be given as a worst-case value for all R or as a function of R. Because a node may have multiple inputs and complex internal scheduling, the j-th EF packet to arrive at the node destined for a certain interface may not be the j-th EF packet to depart from that interface, and the first pair of equations is unaware of packet identity.

The second pair of equations is the same but tracks individual packets. D_j is the actual departure time of the individual EF packet that arrived at the node destined for the interface at time A_j, and F_j is its target departure time, with the same recursion and the same terms for packet size, rate and error. Here the error term is E_p, the deviation for individual packets. It is the fact that D_j and F_j refer to departure times for the j-th packet to arrive that makes this pair of equations aware of packet identity, and that is the critical distinction between the two pairs.

The node should be able to be characterized by the range of R values and the value of E_p it can meet, and an E_p value of undefined may be specified. The revised specification also recommends that a compliant node should not reorder packets within a microflow.
sections.plainLanguage: The behaviour is stated as a schedule. For each EF packet the router computes the moment the packet ought to leave the link, and the equations say the real departure must be within an error term of that moment. One pair of equations judges the traffic as a whole, and a second pair judges each packet on its own.

sections.title: Why Two Characterizations
sections.content:
Consider an ideal output-buffered device with an EF FIFO at the output. For such a device the i-th packet to arrive is also the i-th packet to depart, so the aggregate behaviour and the packet-identity-aware characteristics are identical and E_a equals E_p. In that case the memo omits the subscript and calls the latency term simply E.

For such an ideal device the new definition is stronger than the well-known rate-latency curve: if a scheduler satisfies the EF definition it also satisfies the rate-latency curve, and so all the properties known for that curve also apply. The rate-latency curve is defined as D(j) at most F'(j) plus E, where F'(0) is zero and F'(j) is the maximum of a(j) and F'(j-1) plus L(j) divided by R. The difference is that F'(j) is the time the j-th departure should have occurred if the EF aggregate were constantly served exactly at its configured rate R, which the memo calls the fluid finish time. The intuitive meaning is that any packet is served at most time E later than it would finish service in the fluid model.

The rate-latency curve guarantees the desired rate in any interval to within a specified error, but it may result in large gaps in service. Suppose N identical EF packets of length L arrive from different interfaces to the EF queue with no non-EF traffic. Any work-conserving scheduler serves all N at link speed, so when the last packet is sent at time NL divided by C, the fluid finish time of the Nth packet equals NL divided by R, and the scheduler is running ahead of ideal. If a large number of non-EF packets then arrive at that moment, followed by a single EF packet, the scheduler can legitimately delay starting to send the EF packet until the fluid finish time of the next packet. The EF aggregate then has no service at all in that interval, and the interval can be quite large if R is substantially smaller than C. In essence the EF aggregate can be punished by a gap in service for receiving faster service than its configured rate at the beginning.

The new definition alleviates this by introducing the term min(D(j-1), F(j-1)) into the recursion, which resets the fluid finishing time if a packet is sent before its ideal departure time. As a consequence, for the case where the EF aggregate is served in FIFO order, a packet arriving at time t is transmitted no later than time t plus Q(t) divided by R plus E, where Q(t) is the EF queue size at time t including the packet in question.

Where the output scheduler does not serve EF packets in FIFO order, or internal delay reorders packets, or both, the two definitions are no longer identical. The memo's analogy for the aggregate part is a dark reservoir into which all arriving packets are placed, and a scheduler is allowed to pick packets from it in a random order without any knowledge of the arrival order. The aggregate part measures the accuracy of the output rate provided to the EF aggregate as a whole, and the smaller E_a is, the more accurate the assurance that the reservoir is drained at least at the configured rate. The definition of the EF behaviour explicitly forbids reordering within a microflow, which restricts the scheduling implementation, or in the analogy the order of pulling packets out of the reservoir, but still allows reordering at the aggregate level.

Reordering within the aggregate is not necessarily a bad service. A scheduler that arbitrates among ten EF flows with diverse rates may send a packet of the faster flow before one of the slower flow to keep jitter low at the flow level, and an ideal flow-aware weighted fair queuing scheduler will cause reordering within the aggregate while maintaining packet ordering and small jitter at the flow level.

The small value of E_a gives no assurance about the absolute value of per-packet delay, and if the input rate exceeds the configured rate the aggregate behaviour definition may result in arbitrarily large delay for a subset of packets. That is the primary motivation for the packet-identity-aware definition, whose goal is to provide a way to find a per-packet delay bound as a function of input traffic parameters. The value of E_p is affected by two factors, the accuracy of the aggregate rate service and the degree of packet reordering within the EF aggregate, under the constraint that packets within the same microflow are not reordered. A device that gives an ideal service rate to the aggregate and to each sub-aggregate may still have a very large E_p, in which case E_p must be at least the ratio of the maximum packet size to the smallest rate of any sub-aggregate. So a large E_p does not necessarily mean the service is bad; it may indicate that the service is good but non-FIFO. A small E_p does indicate a high quality FIFO implementation. Since E_p and E_a relate to different aspects, they should be considered together to judge the quality of the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The two error terms measure different things. One says how well the router kept to the rate it promised for EF traffic as a whole. The other says how far any one packet wandered from its own schedule. A router can score well on the first and badly on the second, and that usually means it served the traffic well but out of order, not that it served it badly.

sections.title: Delay and Loss
sections.content:
The primary motivation for the packet-identity-aware definition is that it allows the per-packet delay bound to be quantified. If the total traffic arriving to an output port from all inputs is constrained by a leaky bucket with parameters R and B, where R is the configured rate and B is the bucket depth, then the delay of any packet departing from that port is bounded by B divided by R plus E_p.

Because the bound depends on the configured rate and the input burstiness, it is desirable for both to be visible to a user of the device. A policy-based discriminator desiring a particular delay bound may need to limit the range of configured rates and allowed burstiness it can support in order to deliver such a bound, and the equation provides a means of determining an acceptable operating region for a given E_p. It may also be useful to limit the total offered load to an output to some rate below the configured rate, for example to obtain end-to-end delay bounds, although the delay bound itself does not depend on that limit.

On multi-hop delay, the behaviour is inherently local, but it is tempting to conclude that the bound across h hops is simply h times the single-hop bound. That is not necessarily the case unless B represents the worst case input burstiness across all nodes in the network, and obtaining such a worst case value is not trivial. If EF is implemented using aggregate class-based scheduling where all EF packets share a single FIFO, the effect of jitter accumulation may increase burstiness from hop to hop. It can be shown that, unless severe restrictions on EF utilization are imposed, even if all EF flows are ideally shaped at the ingress, then for any value of delay D it is possible to construct a network where EF utilization on any link is bounded, no flow traverses more than a specified number of hops, but a packet exists that experiences a delay greater than D. Limiting the worst case burstiness and the resulting end-to-end delay may therefore require not only limiting EF utilization on all links but also constraining the global network topology, which would have to be specified in the definition of any policy-based discriminator built on EF if it requires a strict worst case delay bound.

On packet loss, any device with finite buffering may need to drop packets if the input burstiness becomes sufficiently high. To meet the low loss objective of EF, a node may be characterized by the operating region in which loss due to congestion will not occur, which may be specified as a token bucket of rate r not greater than R and burst size B that can be offered from all inputs to a given output interface without loss. Because of jitter accumulation it is generally difficult to guarantee that the input burstiness never exceeds that region for nodes internal to the domain, so a no-loss guarantee across multiple hops may need topology constraints outside the scope of a local definition. It must therefore be possible to establish whether a device conforms even when some packets are lost. That can be done by performing an off-line test of conformance: after observing a sequence of packets entering and leaving the node, the packets that did not leave are assumed lost and notionally removed from the input stream, and conformance is verified by considering only the packets that passed through. Which packets are lost when loss does occur is beyond the scope of the definition, but those that were not lost must conform to the equations.
sections.plainLanguage: Given a configured rate and a bound on how bursty the incoming traffic is, the equations give a bound on how long any packet can wait. Across several routers that bound does not simply add up, because each hop makes the traffic burstier, so a strict end-to-end figure needs limits on the network as well as on the devices.

sections.title: Scheduler Examples
sections.content:
A packet passing through a router experiences delay for a number of reasons. Two familiar components are the time it spends in a buffer at an outgoing link waiting for the scheduler to select it and the time it takes to actually transmit it on the outgoing line. There may be others: a router might have to do header processing before the packet can be given to the output scheduler, or the packet may sit in a transmission queue after being selected but before it is transmitted. In such cases the extra delay can be accounted for by absorbing it into the latency terms.

Implementing EF on a router with a multi-stage switch fabric requires special attention, because a packet may experience additional delays from competing with other traffic for forwarding resources at multiple contention points in the switch core. The delay before the packet even reaches the output-link scheduler should be included in the latency term, and input-buffered and input/output-buffered routers based on crossbar design may also require modification of their latency terms, because the speedup factor and the choice of crossbar arbitration algorithms can affect the latency terms substantially. Core delay has a fixed part, including the time for packet segmentation and reassembly in cell based cores, enqueueing and dequeuing at each stage and transmission between stages, and a variable part that depends on the type and amount of other traffic traversing the core. Some of that competing traffic may even come from other, non-EF aggregates.

The memo works through two simplified implementation examples. The first is an ideal output-buffered node where packets entering the device from an input interface are immediately delivered to the output scheduler, so that the properties of the output scheduler fully define E_a and E_p. The second is a router modelled as a black box with a known bound on the variable delay a packet can experience from the time it arrives at an input to the time it is delivered to its destination output, with the output scheduler assumed to be an aggregate scheduler where all EF packets share a single FIFO queue.

For the output-buffered model, a strict priority scheduler in which all EF packets share a single FIFO queue served at strict non-preemptive priority over other queues satisfies the EF definition with the latency term E equal to the maximum packet size divided by the speed of the output link. A class-based WF2Q scheduler in which all EF traffic shares a single queue with the weight corresponding to the configured rate of the EF aggregate satisfies the definition with E equal to the maximum packet size divided by the link speed plus the maximum packet size divided by the configured rate. For Deficit Round Robin, E can be shown to grow linearly with the number of queues times the ratio of the largest to the smallest rate assignment times the maximum packet size. For Start-Time Fair Queuing and Self-Clocked Fair Queuing, E grows linearly with the number of queues in the scheduler.

For the router with internal delay, the computation of E_p is more complicated. If a packet entering the router may experience a variable delay D_v with a known upper bound D, and the output scheduler has a known value E(S), then E_p equals E(S) plus twice D plus twice B divided by R. In the absence of a bound on B, E_p can be bounded as E(S) plus D times the input rate divided by R. These bounds use only the bound on the variable portion of the interval delay and the error bound of the output scheduler; with more detail about the device architecture, better bounds may be computed.
sections.plainLanguage: Whatever scheduler a router uses, the numbers in the definition have to work out for that router. The memo works them out for a strict priority queue, for WF2Q, for Deficit Round Robin and for the fair queuing family, and then adds the delay a real router adds inside its switch fabric. The fair queuing schedulers scale badly: the more queues a router has, the worse the latency term becomes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it provides additional information to aid understanding of the EF behaviour described in RFC 3246, that it adds no new functions to it, and that as a result it adds no security issues to those described in that specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the memo changes nothing about how EF works, it raises no security questions of its own.

viz.caption: THE TWO PAIRS OF EQUATIONS AS PRINTED IN THE RFC

data.title: The EF definition
data.code:
d_j <= f_j + E_a for all j>0                                (eq_1)

where f_j is defined iteratively by

f_0 = 0, d_0 = 0

f_j = max(a_j, min(d_j-1, f_j-1)) + l_j/R,  for all j > 0   (eq_2)

D_j <= F_j + E_p for all j>0                                (eq_3)

where F_j is defined iteratively by

F_0 = 0, D_0 = 0

F_j = max(A_j, min(D_j-1, F_j-1)) + L_j/R,  for all j > 0   (eq_4)

items.title: E_a, the aggregate term
items.text: How far the actual departure of EF traffic as a whole may be from its ideal departure.

items.title: E_p, the per-packet term
items.text: How far the actual departure of one packet may be from its own ideal departure.

items.title: Why both are needed
items.text: The aggregate term says nothing about the delay of an individual packet, and the per-packet term cannot tell whether the rate was accurate.

items.title: What a large E_p means
items.text: Not necessarily bad service; it may mean good service that is not FIFO.
